blocks.text: Where a systems analyst's day goes

Start with the work itself. O*NET, the U.S. Department of Labor's occupation database, lists the main tasks for computer systems analysts. Those tasks include troubleshooting program and system malfunctions, helping users with computer problems, testing and monitoring systems, and analyzing business problems with computers. Most of that work involves other people.

The frequency data tells you more than the task list. Email shows up every day for every respondent. Telephone conversations happen every day for 79%. About 73% say they are in constant contact with others. And 53% say they sit continually or almost continually. A day built on those numbers is a day of messages, calls and screens, with little room for quiet work.

blocks.caption: Work context frequencies for occupation 15-1211.00, from O*NET OnLine.

blocks.text: Read these figures with care. O*NET gives how often each activity happens, not how many hours it takes. Microsoft's 2023 Work Trend Index gives hours, but for all commercial workers, not analysts. It finds that 57% of time goes to communicating, and email is about 15% of time. The heaviest email users, the top 25 percent, spend 8.8 hours a week on it. Use those figures as a rough guide. Track your own week for a week or two to get a real picture.
Email for systems analysts on Mac: the first hour

Start in Outlook for Mac, and check your version first. Open Outlook > About Microsoft Outlook. Microsoft's release notes list version 16.114 (Build 26101123) from October 14, 2026. The October 22 and October 27 entries list only quality and performance improvements. If your build is older, update before you rely on a feature list from a blog.

Microsoft's Outlook for Mac support page lists features that matter to analysts. Snooze lets you push a message back to a later time. The Calendar has a 3-day view. My Day shows your agenda in a task pane in Mail. MailTips warns you about large Reply All lists and about sensitive content sent outside your organization. Read those warnings. They catch the Reply All that sends a log dump to the wrong group.

items: ⌘N starts a new message.
⌘R replies to the sender.
⇧⌘R replies to everyone on the thread.
Check the To and Cc lines before every send, especially on a vendor thread.

blocks.text: Lazur fits in the gap between reading and replying. Hold ⌥ ⌘ over a long thread and ask what the sender needs from you. Lazur reads what is on screen and answers out loud. Ask it to point at Snooze if you cannot find it. Lazur circles the control and labels it. You still click.

Dictation saves more time than most people expect. Hold fn and speak, and Lazur types clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Use it for a reply to a vendor or a note on a ticket. Then read the text before you send it. Dictated text reads well even when one service name or ID is wrong.
Calls, meetings and the communication load

Calls are the second large block. O*NET reports that 79% of analysts have telephone conversations every day. Add the 73% who report constant contact with others, and the day fills before lunch. Atlassian's State of Teams 2024 estimates about 25 billion work hours a year are lost to ineffective collaboration across the Fortune 500. That survey covers 5,000 knowledge workers and 100 Fortune 500 executives, so treat the figure as a signal, not a count.

A common pattern goes like this. A meeting ends. The decisions live in your head. The status update goes out late, and it is vague. Break that pattern right after the call. Hold fn and dictate the decisions, the owners and the open questions. Then ask Lazur to draft the status message from what you said. Read it, edit it, and send it under your name.

Atlassian also reports that 65% of knowledge workers say quick responses matter more than progress on top priorities. Quick replies feel productive. They can also break up the long, quiet stretches that testing and analysis need. Pick fixed times for replies, and tell your team when they are.

blocks.title: Check before you send
blocks.text: Read names, numbers and service IDs by eye before you send dictated or drafted text. Those are the details a fluent draft can get wrong without any sign.
Troubleshooting and testing with an AI assistant on screen

Troubleshooting is the core of the job. O*NET lists troubleshooting program and system malfunctions among the top main tasks. Many sessions start with an error on screen. It sits in a log viewer, a dashboard or a vendor console. An assistant that reads the screen saves you from copying each line into a chat window by hand.

Lazur explains what is on screen. Hold ⌥ ⌘ over the error and ask what it means. Lazur answers out loud and can point at the line it means. That helps when a stack trace runs long and you need the first failing call. Ask it to explain, then check the answer against the system. Lazur only sees what is visible. It can be wrong about the cause.

Testing needs the same care. When you run a test plan by hand, ask Lazur to read the expected result from the page and compare it with the screen. Let it help with the wording of test steps. Write the final steps yourself. Keep a dated record of what you checked and what you saw.

blocks.title: Production data on screen
blocks.text: Logs and dashboards often show customer names, email addresses or account numbers. Follow your employer's rules on that data before you ask about it. Hide anything you do not need. A privacy note from a tool does not give you permission to share it.
Excel for systems analysts: exports, duplicates and pivots

Analysts live inside exports. A vendor sends a file, you open it in Excel for Mac, and something looks wrong. Start by finding the bad cells. Use Formulas > Formula Auditing > Trace Precedents to see which cells feed a formula. Then decide whether the data or the formula is at fault.

Here is a common case. A column of counts shows a #VALUE error in a few rows. Open the formula bar and read what the cell adds or multiplies. A frequent cause is text from the vendor, such as 'n/a', sitting in a cell the formula treats as a number. Ask Lazur to point at the cell and explain it. The demo on this page shows that moment.

Duplicates are the next trap. Select the range, then choose Data > Remove Duplicates. Excel asks which columns define a duplicate. Choose them with care. Two rows can match on ticket ID and still be separate events with different timestamps. Save a copy of the raw export before you remove anything.

For summaries, use Insert > PivotTable. A field list confuses many people, so ask Lazur to guide you through the first pivot. Lazur guides you one click at a time and waits for each click. That suits a pivot, because a wrong field in the wrong box gives a clean table that answers the wrong question.
For more on formulas and pivots, read [Excel for computer systems analysts on Mac](/for/computer-systems-analysts/excel).
Writing user guides and training notes with AI

The Bureau of Labor Statistics lists writing instruction manuals and training end users among the duties of computer systems analysts. It also lists consulting with managers about the role of IT systems, and testing systems to confirm they work as expected. Those tasks produce a lot of prose. Most of it repeats, with small changes for each audience.

Use Lazur for the first draft. Dictate what the system does in plain speech. Then ask for a one-page guide for a named audience, such as finance staff who run a month-end report. Lazur drafts the text and types it where your cursor sits. Check every step against the real system. A draft can sound right and still name the wrong menu.

Two mistakes show up often. The first is pasting a draft into a user guide without a test run. The second is writing one draft for every audience. Managers need the risk and the impact. Users need button names and what to expect. Ask for both versions and keep them apart.

items: Dictate the purpose and the audience in one breath.
Ask for numbered steps and a short troubleshooting section.
Walk each step on the real system and fix any names that differ.
Save the final guide in your team's wiki, not on your Mac's desktop.

blocks.text: Tickets, specs and wikis in Notion, Linear and Confluence

Your ticket system and wiki are where specs go stale. O*NET's tool list for this occupation includes Confluence, SharePoint, Git, Tableau and Power BI. Each one holds a piece of the truth, and none of them updates itself.

Lazur reads the page you have open. Ask it to list open questions in a spec, or to explain a field you keep misreading. It cannot update the ticket or edit the page. You paste or type the changes. That keeps the record accurate.

If your team tracks requests in Notion, a database with a status property works well. See [how to create a database in Notion on Mac](/how-to/create-a-database-in-notion). If your team uses Linear, read [Linear for computer systems analysts on Mac](/for/computer-systems-analysts/linear) for intake and shortcut ideas.
Mac tool sprawl: what the official lists leave out

The tool lists for this occupation read like a Windows and Microsoft shop. O*NET names Outlook, Exchange, Teams, Excel, PowerPoint, SharePoint and Git. It does not mention macOS. If you work on a Mac, the vendor's own pages are your source for Mac behavior. Start with the support page for each app, not a blog post.

Microsoft's Outlook for Mac support page says support for legacy Outlook for Mac will end in October 2026. That date has passed as of this writing. Check which Outlook you run, and check the page for current status. The same page lists Notes and Tasks views as not yet available in the new Outlook, so test those views before you switch.

blocks.title: Check the page date
blocks.text: Check the date on every vendor page before you act on it. A feature list written a year ago can describe an app that has since changed.
Client data, production data and your employer's rules

Here is how Lazur handles data. It listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so Lazur can answer you. They are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

That covers Lazur's side only. It does not decide what you may share. Your employer decides that. Systems analysts often see production data, customer records and security logs. Company policy, data handling rules and the IT or security team come first. Ask before you use any AI tool with regulated data.

This page makes no compliance claims for Lazur. Do not read a privacy summary as approval. Hide what you do not need. Crop screenshots, blur account numbers and use test data when you can. Ask Lazur about the logic of an error, not about one customer's record.
Your first week with Lazur on a Mac
Start small. Give each day one task, then decide whether the tool fits your work.

items: Download Lazur from the [download page](/download) and open it on your Mac.
Read each macOS permission prompt before you allow it. You can review them later under System Settings > Privacy & Security.
Hold ⌥ ⌘ over an Outlook thread and ask what the sender needs from you.
Hold fn and dictate a short status note. Read it before you send it.
Open an Excel export and ask Lazur to explain one formula you did not write.
Ask for research on a vendor behavior. Lazur works in its own Chrome tabs through the Lazur for Chrome extension and returns a summary and a report. Read the report before you act.

blocks.text: Mistakes people make with an AI assistant at work

items: Trusting the first answer about a cause. Check the logs and the system before you change anything.
Expecting it to act. Lazur points and guides. It does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you.
Dictating names and IDs into a shared document without a read-through.
Looking for Windows support. Lazur runs on macOS, and Windows is planned, not available.
Pasting client or production data into any tool before you check your employer's rules.
Letting a draft become the guide. Keep your own test notes next to it.

blocks.text: Pricing, trial and what to check before you buy

Lazur has a free trial, and it needs no credit card. The trial starts when you first open the app. The paid plans are Pro and Power. Dictation is unlimited on both. Current prices and AI action limits are on the [pricing page](/pricing), so check them there before you decide.

Ask three questions first. Does it help with the apps you use every day? Can your employer approve it for the data you handle? Do you dictate often? If you do, dictation alone may already be worth the time. If you want a baseline first, try the [typing speed test](/tools/typing-speed-test).
Who this job is and where it is heading
The Bureau of Labor Statistics counted 544,400 computer systems analyst jobs in 2025. The median pay was $105,850 per year in May 2025. Employment is projected to grow 8% from 2025 to 2035.
More analysts will share the same tools, and more of the work will run through screens and messages. Whatever you use, keep one habit. Check the source, check the system, then send.

faq.question: Is there an AI assistant for systems analysts on Mac?
faq.answer: Lazur is a voice assistant for macOS that works in any app. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about what is on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It explains, points and guides. It does not click buttons or edit files for you.

faq.question: Does Lazur work with Outlook for Mac?
faq.answer: Lazur sees what is on your screen, so you can ask about an Outlook for Mac message while it is open. Lazur is not a plugin or add-in for Outlook, and it has no partnership with any app maker. It can draft a reply that you paste or dictate.

faq.question: Can Lazur edit my Excel file or my tickets?
faq.answer: No. Lazur explains, points and guides. You make the change yourself. It drafts text and types it at your cursor when you ask, but it does not edit files or operate other apps.

faq.question: Does Lazur watch my screen all the time?
faq.answer: No. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so Lazur can answer. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models.

faq.question: Can I use Lazur with client or patient data?
faq.answer: Follow your employer's rules first. A privacy summary from Lazur does not replace approval from your IT or security team. This page makes no compliance claims for Lazur. Ask before you put regulated data on screen.

faq.question: Does Lazur run on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available.

faq.question: Where can I check prices?
faq.answer: Check the [pricing page](/pricing). It lists the free trial, the Pro and Power plans and the AI action limits for each. Dictation is unlimited on both paid plans.
